slides.text: The presentation is by Sergey Nikolenko.
The presentation is at Harbour Space University.
The presentation date is June 23, 2026.
On June 23, 1314, the Battle of Bannockburn began near Stirling.
In the Battle of Bannockburn, Robert the Bruce's heavily outnumbered Scots routed the much larger English army of Edward II.
The Battle of Bannockburn secured Scottish independence for a generation.
On June 23, 1868, Christopher Latham Sholes patented the 'Type-Writer'.
To stop the mechanical type-bars from jamming, Christopher Latham Sholes scattered the letters into the QWERTY layout.
The QWERTY layout is deliberately awkward.
We are all still typing on the QWERTY layout a century and a half later.
On June 23, 1894, Baron Pierre de Coubertin convened a congress at the Sorbonne.
The congress at the Sorbonne founded the International Olympic Committee.
The congress at the Sorbonne resolved to revive the Olympic Games.
June 23 is celebrated as Olympic Day every year since 1894.
On June 23, 1926, the College Board administered the first SAT exam.
The SAT exam is still a landmark for US students.
On June 23, 1991, Sega released Sonic the Hedgehog in North America.
Sonic the Hedgehog was engineered to be faster and edgier than Nintendo's Mario.
For a few years, Sonic the Hedgehog pushed Sega ahead of Nintendo in the U.S. console war.
GAN stands for Generative Adversarial Networks.
GAN involves a generator and a discriminator.
GAN contrasts p_data and p_g.
Ideally, GAN training proceeds as described by Geitgey (2017).
At first, the generator is bad.
At first, the discriminator can't do anything either.
In ideal GAN training, first the discriminator is trained a little.
Then the generator has to come up with something better.
The GAN training process continues until everything works out.
Formally, the generator is a function G = G(z; θ_g) from Z to X.
The discriminator is a function D = D(x; θ_d) from X to [0,1].
The discriminator's objective function is binary classification: E_{x~p_data(x)} [log D(x)] + E_{x~p_g(x)} [log(1 - D(x))].
p_g(x) = G_{z~p_z(z)} is the distribution generated by G.
In training, we take two mini-batches, with labels 0 from the generator and labels 1 from the data.
The generator learns to fool the discriminator by minimizing E_{x~p_g(x)}[log(1 - D(x))] = E_{z~p_z(z)}[log(1 - D(G(z)))].
Combining generator and discriminator objectives gives a minimax game: min_G max_D V(D,G), where V(D,G) = E_{x~p_data(x)}[log D(x)] + E_{z~p_z(z)}[log(1 - D(G(z)))].
It can be proven that max_D V(D,G) is minimized exactly when p_g = p_data.
For a fixed generator G, the optimal discriminator distribution D^*_G(x) = p_data(x) / (p_data(x) + p_g(x)).
The global minimum of the criterion is attained if and only if p_g = p_data.
For the optimal D, the criterion is equivalent to KL(p_data || (p_data + p_g)/2) + KL(p_g || (p_data + p_g)/2), which is the Jensen-Shannon divergence.
These results are for the generator loss E_{z~p_z(z)}[log(1 - D(G(z)))].
This generator loss is not the best loss function for the generator.
The problem with minimizing E_{z~p_z(z)}[log(1 - D(G(z)))] is examined.
Cross-entropy is good in a classifier: if the answer is wrong, it does not saturate; if it is right, it saturates and does not change.
In GANs, when the discriminator works well, its gradient vanishes.
Then the generator gradient also vanishes.
Hence, in practice we minimize -E_{z~p_z(z)}[log D(G(z))], i.e., maximize the probability that D made a mistake, rather than minimizing the probability of D's correct answer.
GAN training is essentially similar to the EM algorithm, alternating between updating discriminator and generator.
When updating the discriminator, we fix G and use loss function E_{x~p_data(x)} [log D(x)] + E_{x~p_g(x)} [log(1 - D(x))].
When updating the generator, we fix D and use loss function -E_{x~p_data(x)}[log D(x)].
The discriminator tries to recognize.
The generator wants to generate.
There is a method for sampling from a GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014).
DCGAN stands for Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks, introduced by Radford et al., 2016.
DCGAN uses several new tricks: strided convolutions instead of pooling, batchnorm everywhere, removing fully connected layers, and using Adam optimizer.
DCGAN generated bedrooms from LSUN dataset after one epoch.
DCGAN generated bedrooms from LSUN dataset after five epochs.
DCGAN allows a walk through its feature space.
Removing filters that detect windows in DCGAN is demonstrated.
DCGAN supports vector arithmetic, similar to word2vec.
Geitgey (2017) used DCGAN to generate pixel art from NES games.
There is an animation of pixel art generation at https://medium.com/@ageitgey/abusing-generative-adversarial-networks-to-make-8-bit-pixel-art-e45d9b96cee7.
DCGAN does not always work; it has problems with counting.
DCGAN has problems with perspective.
The very first GANs worked as described.
Since then, significant progress has been made in GANs.
The slide asks how that progress happened.
An important breakthrough in GANs came from NVIDIA in Karras et al., 2017.
This breakthrough introduced Progressive Growing GAN (ProGAN).
In ProGAN, at each stage the GAN is trained to create images four times larger, starting from 4×4.
By progressively growing, the resolution increases up to 1024×1024.
In ProGAN, new layers are added each time.
The discriminator in ProGAN is roughly symmetric to the generator.
ProGAN's progressive growing helps save training time and shows more data in the same time.
There are video demonstrations of ProGAN at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G06dEcZ-QTg and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=36lE9tV9vm0.
For other categories, ProGAN did not go all the way to 1024×1024, but 256×256 resolution looks pretty good.
ProGAN is trained in a fairly standard way; the authors compared loss functions of least squares GAN and Wasserstein GAN.
The presentation then says 'let's figure it out' regarding those loss functions.
LSGAN stands for Least Squares GAN, introduced by Mao et al., 2016.
The problem with ordinary GANs is that the loss function (Jensen-Shannon divergence) saturates when the generator distribution is far from the correct one, leading to no training.
This is because the discriminator in an ordinary GAN works like a classifier with a logistic sigmoid.
In LSGAN, the discriminator minimizes the loss: 1/2 𝔼x∼𝑝data [(𝐷(x) −𝑏)²] + 1/2 𝔼z∼𝑝z [(𝐷(𝐺(z)) −𝑎)²].
In LSGAN, the generator minimizes the loss: 1/2 𝔼z∼𝑝z [(𝐷(𝐺(z)) −𝑐)²].
The discriminator learns to output value 𝑎 for fake data and 𝑏 for real data.
The generator wants the discriminator to output value 𝑐 for fake data.
Typically, the target values are set as 𝑎=0, 𝑏=1, and 𝑐=1.
Mao et al. showed that LSGAN is more robust to changes in architecture.
Mao et al. showed that LSGAN suffers less from mode collapse.
The quadratic loss function is now often used.
InfoGAN was introduced by Chen et al. in 2016.
InfoGAN aims to learn interpretable representations by information maximizing.
InfoGAN seeks to add disentanglement so that different features have meaning.
In ordinary GANs, the generator uses a noise vector z.
In InfoGAN, the input to the generator is split into two parts: z and c.
In InfoGAN, z is the incompressible noise source of entropy.
In InfoGAN, c = 𝑐₁𝑐₂ … 𝑐𝐿 is the latent code.
When using a generator 𝐺(z, c), an additional mechanism is needed to ensure that the latent code c is not ignored by the generator.
InfoGAN requires high mutual information between the latent code c and the generator output 𝐺(z, c).
The mutual information goal is implemented via a variational lower bound.
The variational lower bound is parametrized with a neural network 𝑄 using the reparametrization trick.
The network 𝑄 usually almost entirely coincides with the discriminator 𝐷.
An InfoGAN experiment on MNIST uses a latent code c consisting of three parts: 𝑐₁, 𝑐₂, 𝑐₃.
In the MNIST example, 𝑐₁ is a discrete categorical variable with 10 categories and a uniform prior distribution, learned without supervision.
In the MNIST example, 𝑐₂ and 𝑐₃ are uniformly distributed on [−1, 1].
Using the latent code 𝑐₁, a classifier achieves a 5% error rate on MNIST without any supervision.
InfoGAN can generate 3D faces.
InfoGAN can generate 3D chairs.
Wasserstein GAN was introduced by Arjovsky et al. in 2017.
Learning a probability distribution typically involves minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence KL(𝑝data‖𝑝model).
KL divergence requires that 𝑝model exists, which fails if the model distribution is concentrated on low-dimensional submanifolds.
The manifold of 𝑝model is unlikely to intersect substantially with the manifold of 𝑝data.
When manifolds do not intersect substantially, KL divergence is undefined or infinite.
In practice, noise (e.g., Gaussian) is often added to ensure the model distribution has support everywhere.
In generative models, adding noise can make generated samples blurry.
Noise is typically added during maximum likelihood training but removed during generation, meaning the noise is not part of the desired distribution but is necessary for training.
Wasserstein GAN considers alternative metrics of closeness between data and model distributions.
The Wasserstein-1 distance, also called Earth Mover distance, is defined as 𝑊(𝑝data, 𝑝model) = inf_{𝛾∈Π(𝑝data,𝑝model)} 𝔼(x,y)∼𝛾[‖x − y‖].
Π(𝑝data, 𝑝model) denotes the set of all joint distributions 𝛾(x, y) with marginals 𝑝data and 𝑝model.
The joint distribution 𝛾(x, y) indicates how much probability mass must be moved from x to y to transform 𝑝data into 𝑝model.
Consider an example where 𝑍 is uniformly distributed on [0,1], ℙ₀ is the distribution of (0, 𝑍) in ℝ², and the generator is defined as 𝑔𝜃(𝑧) = (𝜃, 𝑧) with parameter 𝜃.
In this example, only the Earth Mover (EM) distance converges as 𝜃 → 0, unlike other distances.
This behavior resembles learning a distribution concentrated on a submanifold.
The Wasserstein distance 𝑊(𝑝data, 𝑝model) is a continuous function of the parameters of 𝑝model under weak conditions.

By the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality, the Wasserstein distance equals the supremum over 1-Lipschitz functions of the difference in expectations: 𝑊 = sup_{‖𝑓‖_𝐿≤1} (𝔼x∼𝑝data [𝑓(x)] − 𝔼x∼𝑝model [𝑓(x)]).
In the WGAN framework, the generative model is defined as 𝑝model = 𝑔𝜃(z).
Both the function 𝑓 and the generator 𝑔 are parametrized with neural networks.
The function 𝑓 is implemented as a neural network with weights w, and the generator as a network with parameters 𝜃.
Given a fixed generator 𝑔𝜃, the critic 𝑓w is trained to maximize the difference 𝔼x∼𝑝data [𝑓(x)] − 𝔼x∼𝑝model [𝑓(x)].
Given a fixed critic 𝑓w, the gradient of the Wasserstein distance with respect to generator parameters is computed as ∇𝜃𝑊 = −𝔼z∼𝑍[∇𝜃𝑓w(𝑔𝜃(z))].
To enforce the Lipschitz constraint on 𝑓w, weight clipping is applied to the critic's gradients.
In WGAN, the critic can be trained to convergence safely.
In an ordinary GAN, training the discriminator to convergence is not advisable.
In Wasserstein GAN, the quality of generated samples is closely correlated with the value of the loss function.
Wasserstein GAN is more robust to changes in architecture compared to ordinary GAN.
Gulrajani et al. (2017) proposed an improved training method for Wasserstein GANs.
Weight clipping in the critic causes problems such as failure to learn high-order moments of distributions and vanishing/exploding gradients.
A gradient penalty regularizer of the form 𝜆𝔼̂x∼𝑃̂x [(‖∇̂x𝐷(̂x)‖₂ −1)²] is preferred over weight clipping.
Zhang et al. (2019) introduced Self-Attention Generative Adversarial Networks (SAGAN).
SAGAN addresses the problem of locality in generating images with convolutional networks by using self-attention.
The self-attention mechanism in SAGAN is similar to that in the Transformer but adapted for images.
In SAGAN, the generator can attend to distant regions when generating an image, as illustrated by attention maps from the last layer.
The original SAGAN paper demonstrated that the generated images are of high quality.
BigGAN, introduced by Brock et al. in 2019, improved the Inception score threefold compared to previous methods.
BigGAN uses a self-attention GAN with additional tricks and special architectures.
Assessing the quality of generated images is difficult.
The Inception score, introduced by Salimans et al. in 2016, is a metric for evaluating GANs.
To compute the Inception score, generated images are fed into a standard Inception classifier.
The Inception score aims to have low entropy for the conditional distribution 𝑝(𝑦∣x) and high entropy for the marginal distribution 𝑝(𝑦) over generated samples.
The Inception score is defined as exp(𝔼x KL(𝑝(𝑦∣x) || 𝑝(𝑦))).
The Inception score is effective for quality assessment but difficult to use directly for training.
Adversarial autoencoders (AAE) were introduced by Makhzani et al. in 2015.
In an AAE, the discriminator enforces that the distribution of hidden layer features matches a target distribution 𝑝(z).
By making the distributions in AAE conditional, one can achieve semi-supervised learning.
Kadurin et al. (2017) applied adversarial autoencoders to generate molecules for oncology.
Kadurin et al. (2018) developed druGAN, a generative model for molecules, and compared it with VAE.
Polikovsky et al. (2018) introduced MOSES, a platform for comparing generative models for molecules.
Conditional GANs were introduced by Mirza and Osindero in 2014.
In a conditional GAN, the generator receives both a random noise vector and an input condition vector.
Antipov et al. (2017) used a conditional GAN to synthesize aged faces.
Ledig et al. (2017) proposed ESRGAN for image super-resolution.
Stacking multiple GANs sequentially is often useful.
Huang et al. (2017) proposed Stacked Generative Adversarial Networks (SGAN).
In stacked GANs, each generator 𝐺𝑖 learns lower-level representations sequentially by inverting a deep encoder network 𝐸𝑖.
The conditional loss in stacked GANs is defined as ℒcond = 𝔼h𝑖+1∼𝑝data,z𝑖∼𝑝z𝑖[𝑑(𝐸𝑖(𝐺𝑖(h𝑖+1, z𝑖)), h𝑖+1].
The conditional loss ensures that the generator does not ignore the conditioning by reconstructing h𝑖+1 through the encoder.
The entropy loss in stacked GANs is defined as ℒent = 𝔼z𝑖∼𝑝z𝑖[𝔼̂h𝑖∼𝐺𝑖(̂h𝑖∣z𝑖) [−log 𝑄𝑖(z𝑖∣̂ h𝑖)]].
The entropy loss encourages the generator to utilize the noise z by maximizing entropy.
𝑄𝑖 is a neural network that approximates the posterior distribution 𝑝𝑖(z𝑖∣̂ h𝑖) to provide a variational bound.
Stacked GANs produce better results than previous methods, though progressive growing is still better.

Even in two lectures, it is possible to cover a couple of very interesting, very important, and very relevant ideas.
Today's lecture topic is generative adversarial networks (GANs).
The idea underlying GANs is beautiful and completely non-mathematical.
The idea underlying GANs is very cool and very logical.
The idea underlying GANs leads to very beautiful mathematics later on.
Before discussing GANs, the lecture will begin with the structure of generative AI as a whole.
The first part of today's lecture will be about generative models in general and the kinds of generative models that exist in deep learning.
The term 'generative AI' or 'generative models' is not very well-defined.
Logistic regression can be said to generate a probability distribution over classes.
The defining characteristic of generative AI is that it produces something big.
Generative AI produces objects usually of high dimension and complicated structure, such as images or text.
Generative models are models that write, draw, produce music, videos, or similar outputs.
The first subject for discussion is a taxonomy of generative models.
The discussion will be limited to deep generative models.
Deep generative models are models based on neural networks.
There are several important classes of deep generative models.
Today's lecture will cover one class of deep generative models, and tomorrow's lecture will cover another class.
Drawing a general taxonomy helps to better understand deep generative models.
The first major distinction in deep generative models is between explicit density models and implicit density models.
A generative model takes as input something like random noise or a condition.
The generative model is a black box that we are trying to define.
The output of a generative model is something like a picture of a cat.
The output X lives in a very high dimensional space.
X has a very complicated distribution.
The instructor previously made the argument about imagining the manifold of realistic photos in a high-dimensional space.
1 megapixel images correspond to a 3 million dimensional space.
It is impossible to imagine the manifold of realistic photos in such a high-dimensional space.
The manifold is extremely complicated.
P(X), the distribution of X that we are trying to approximate and model, is very complicated.
In explicit density models, you get an explicit model for the density.
In explicit density models, P(X) is explicitly represented as something in the model, and one can compute it.
We cannot get the actual distribution of cat photos, but we can approximate it.
Inside explicit density models, there is a further divide involving tractable density models.
Tractable density means that you can have a formula for P(X).
Tractable density models make strong assumptions that allow writing down a formula for P(X).
Tractable density usually refers to an autoregressive model.
An autoregressive model makes use of an obvious identity.
For a large X, you can decompose P(X) into a product of conditional probabilities: P(X1) * P(X2|X1) * P(X3|X1,X2) * ... * P(Xn|X1,...,Xn-1).
This decomposition is always true.
The decomposition is always true but completely useless because it remains a very big function of many variables.
You can simplify by making assumptions.
One can make a Markov chain assumption out of this decomposition.
In a Markov chain assumption, every next X depends only on the previous X.
An RNN models a sequence where every next output depends only on the current input and the hidden state.
Using an RNN yields another simplified decomposition.
Many existing models belong to the autoregressive class.
Almost all large language models (LLMs) are autoregressive because they predict the next token.
LLMs model text as a sequence of conditional probabilities p(x_k | previous context).
The question is how to model the conditional distribution.
Transformers and other models are used to model the conditional distribution.
The basic assumption is that text is generated one token at a time.
There have been autoregressive models for pictures.
PixelCNN is an example of an autoregressive model for images.
PixelCNN produced images pixel by pixel and had good output quality.
Producing images pixel by pixel is too inefficient because generating a million pixels requires running the model a million times, which is infeasible.
Pixel-wise autoregressive models are not widely used.
The lecture will not discuss pixel-wise autoregressive models.
Pixel-wise autoregressive models exist.
The pixel-wise autoregressive approach is a natural idea.
For text, basically everything is autoregressive.
The lecture will not have time to talk about intractable density models like flow-based models.
One way to decompose a complicated distribution is to separate the variables inside x (autoregressive style).
Another way is to model p(x) as a composition of simple transformations: f_k ∘ f_{k-1} ∘ ... ∘ f_2 ∘ f_1(z).
In flow-based models, the composition of transformations is modeled explicitly.
Each transformation f is simple, such as adding Gaussian noise or a linear transformation.
Composing many simple transformations enables modeling much more complicated distributions.
This is similar to how neural networks work.
The lecture will unfortunately not discuss flow-based models at all.
Apart from tractable density models, there are approximate density models.
In approximate density models, p(x) is approximated by a simpler distribution q, which factors into something easier.
The main example of approximate density models is variational autoencoders (VAEs).
The lecture probably won't have time to discuss VAEs, but they might be covered tomorrow.
Variational autoencoders represent one of the most important ideas in deep learning: using variational approximations to obtain good loss functions for generative models.
Variational autoencoders are used frequently.
Tomorrow's lecture will cover diffusion models.
Diffusion models usually operate in the latent space of a variational autoencoder.
The explicit density model category is large, varied, and rich, with many different approaches.
The implicit density model category is not as rich, with much fewer examples.
The instructor will not give other examples of implicit density models because they are esoteric.
The main example of implicit density generative models is GANs.
An implicit density model starts with random noise and produces a sample X that is supposed to be drawn from the distribution P(X).
An implicit density model produces a sample cat picture that should be a good cat picture.
Viewing the implicit density model as a transformation of probability distributions from a simple one (like standard Gaussian noise) to a complicated one in a high-dimensional space makes sense.
A black box that samples cat photos does not contain an explicit formula for P(X).
One could generate a trillion examples from the black box and then learn an explicit density model, but that does not count as the black box itself containing the density formula.
The black box itself does not contain the formula for P(X).
GANs are this kind of implicit density model.
The first part of the lecture (about the general structure of generative models) is over.
The instructor might return to this general structure tomorrow.
The lecture will now discuss generative adversarial networks (GANs).
GANs are one possible solution to a very deep problem in generative models.
If we get to YS, we will discuss other solutions to this problem.
The main deep problem in creating a generative model is determining the loss function, i.e., how to score the results.
There are many ways to solve this problem; it is not an open problem.
The generator starts with random noise z taken from some standard distribution.
The random noise z is input to a generator network.
The generator network maps random noise to an output that is supposed to be a cat picture.
The output is denoted \hat{X}, a predicted cat picture, not yet a real cat.
Generating images is formulated as a machine learning problem.
In this machine learning problem, there is a dataset of real X (cat photos).
There is no paired data where each random noise z corresponds to a specific real image X.
You cannot directly compare \hat{X} to a specific X from the training set because you don't know which one it should be similar to.
A dataset pairing random noise with the images they should produce does not exist and never will, because it doesn't make sense.
The goal of learning a generator is to learn the mapping from random noise to images and to achieve a good, relatively simple parameterization in the noise space.
Next week we would be able to just take random noise and still get reasonable cat pictures.
The data is unlabeled.
It is unsupervised learning.
The desired outcome is for the generated image (X head) to be a good cat picture.
The approach of wanting the generated image to be a good cat picture is reasonable and is exactly what will be done.
The deep question is what it means to be a good cat picture.
There is no mathematical function that can determine if a photo is a good cat picture.
Determining if a set of pixels is a good cat picture is something you have to learn yourself.
Learning what a good cat picture is constitutes half of the problem, if not most of the problem.
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) recognize that you need to learn your loss function.
You need to work for learning the loss function.
You do not have a fixed formula for evaluating how catchy an image looks.
The discriminator is a separate network.
The discriminator takes photos as input.
The discriminator performs binary classification as output.
The binary classification determines if the input is fake or real.
Real is labeled as 1 and fake is labeled as 0.
If the discriminator gets a picture produced by the generator, it should classify it as fake (output 0).
Real images can be sampled from the data, such as real cat photos.
Real images are denoted as x_real, and fake images are denoted as x_fake.
If a real picture is fed into the discriminator, the output should be 1.
The generator and discriminator are at odds with each other.
The generator and discriminator have opposing interests.
The discriminator wants to learn to distinguish between real images and images produced by the generator.
The generator wants to fool the discriminator.
This general idea is called adversarial training.
You may hear that GANs are not what they used to be.
For the last few years, GANs have not been at the forefront of image generation.
Images these days are generated by diffusion models.
Diffusion models will be discussed tomorrow.
Adversarial training is very much alive.
In diffusion models, we will see exactly the idea of adversarial training.
We will see a little bit of a GAN embedded into a diffusion model, making it better.
Adversarial training is still a very important idea in machine learning.
Adversarial training appears in many different fields.
The discussion is only about images.
The speaker has intrapictures about GANs.
The main idea of GANs is very simple.
The generator is like forging a picture.
The discriminator is like a detective that needs to decide whether a picture is real.
In the example, the generator is called a reverse deep convolutional neural network.
The generator learns to counterfeit money, specifically to produce pictures of real money.
At first, the generator just produces random noise.
Then the generator produces a very bad counterfeit.
Initially, the discriminator says the bad counterfeit seems legit because it doesn't know any better.
The discriminator is fooled by the bad counterfeit.
We train the discriminator, and it learns to distinguish real from fake.
The discriminator understands that the counterfeit is not real money (American dollars).
The training process is often done by fixing the discriminator after it has trained for a while.
We then train the generator to fool the current version of the discriminator.
The discriminator no longer accepts the generator's counterfeits.
We train the generator a little more to produce a slightly better counterfeit.
The new counterfeit will still be bad.
There is no general loss function that can tell if an image is good.
There is only the specific discriminator that has learned to not be fooled by some attacks.
At this point, the generator produces a better counterfeit.
The discriminator will find other features to discriminate on.
The generator will have to learn to fake those features.
The generator and discriminator are playing a game.
The hope is that the process works as in an idealized image.
In the idealized image, the generator is represented by arrows.
In Z, there is a uniform distribution.
In X, there is a Gaussian distribution (the green Gaussian).
The black dots are the data points.
At first, the Gaussian distribution does not look like the data points.
The blue dashed line represents the discriminator, which is a logistic sigmoid.
The sigmoid curve distinguishes between the two distributions (generated and data).
At a certain point, the discriminator trains, but not to mimic the data, because that is impossible in high dimensions.
Mimicking the data would be possible in low dimensions, but not in the high-dimensional case of pictures.
The generator learns to fool the discriminator instead of mimicking the data.
In the simplified case, the generator only needs to move the Gaussian a little to fool the discriminator.
The generator does not need to go all the way to the data points.
Subsequently, the discriminator will again be able to distinguish between the two bell curves.
Finally, the generator becomes perfect and the discriminator has no idea what to do and just flips a coin.
In real life, it does not work exactly like this, but the idea is the same.
The discriminator loss is denoted as L_D.
The discriminator is supposed to output 0 for fake and 1 for real.
The loss can be expressed in terms of expectations.
For a real photo from the training set, the discriminator should produce a score that goes to positive infinity, making the sigmoid probability go to one.
The loss for real images includes the term -log D(x).
For fake images, x_fake is sampled from the generator's distribution pg(x).
For fake images, the discriminator is supposed to output 0.
The discriminator's loss is minimized with respect to its parameters.
When the generator is fixed, training the discriminator is a straightforward binary classification problem.
The generator is supposed to produce images that the discriminator classifies as real.
The generator cannot influence the loss term for real images.
For the fake images part, the generator's job is opposite to the discriminator's.
The generator starts with random noise.
The generator takes the discriminator loss on its generated outputs and does the opposite.
The discriminator and generator have the same loss function expression.
There is a combined loss function depending on both generator and discriminator parameters.
The discriminator wants to maximize this combined loss function, while the generator wants to minimize it.
This is a minimax game.

In generative AI, x is a very high-dimensional vector of pixel values, living in a very big space.

summary.text: Generative models produce objects of high dimensionality and complex structure — images, text, music, video.
In deep learning, the first major divide lies between explicit density models and implicit density models.
An explicit density model provides a formula for $p(x)$, the probability density of the data.
Even though the true distribution of, for example, cat photos in a multi-million-dimensional pixel space is impossibly complicated, an explicit approximation can be built.
Tractable density models can write down $p(x)$ as a closed-form product of conditional distributions.

The classic example of a tractable density model is an autoregressive model, which decomposes $p(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) = p(x_1) p(x_2 \mid x_1) p(x_3 \mid x_1, x_2) \cdots p(x_n \mid x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$.
The autoregressive decomposition identity is always true.

To make the decomposition useful, simplifying assumptions are introduced, such as a Markov chain, an RNN with a hidden state, or a Transformer that conditions each next token on the preceding context.
All large language models (LLMs) are autoregressive models that generate text one token at a time.
Pixel-wise autoregressive models for images, such as PixelCNN, exist.
Generating a million pixels a million times with pixel-wise autoregressive models is prohibitively slow.
In approximate density models, instead of forcing $p(x)$ itself to be tractable, $p(x)$ is approximated with a simpler distribution $q(x)$ that is easy to handle.
The most important family of approximate density models are Variational Autoencoders (VAEs).
VAEs use variational inference to build a learnable lower bound on the log-likelihood.
VAEs are a cornerstone of generative modelling.
Diffusion models typically operate in the latent space of a VAE.
Flow-based models are an alternative approach that composes many simple, invertible transformations so that the density $p(x)$ can be computed by the change-of-variables formula.
Flow-based models belong to explicit density models.
Flow-based models are not covered in this lecture.
An implicit density model never provides a formula for $p(x)$.
An implicit density model is just a sampler: you feed in random noise and get out a sample $\hat{x}$ that should look like it came from the data distribution.
There is no way to read off a density from a trained implicit density network; you can only draw from it.
The main example of implicit density models is Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).
A generator $G$ maps a random noise vector $z$ drawn from $p_z(z)$, such as a standard Gaussian, to an output $\hat{x}$ that should resemble a real image.
In the generator's training, there is no paired supervision; there is no mapping that specifies which $z$ should produce which particular $x$.
There is no obvious loss function that directly evaluates the quality of a generated image.
The central challenge of generative adversarial networks is how to score the generator's output.
The GAN solution is to learn the loss function itself.

A second network, the discriminator $D$, is introduced; its job is binary classification: it determines whether an image came from the real data distribution $p_{\text{data}}$ (output 1) or from the generator $p_g$ (output 0).
The generator and discriminator have opposing objectives: $D$ wants to tell real from fake, and $G$ wants to fool $D$.
This is called adversarial training.
The generator is defined as $G(z; \theta_g): Z \to X$ and the discriminator as $D(x; \theta_d): X \to [0,1]$.
The discriminator maximizes the log-likelihood of correct classification given by $L_D = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g(x)}[\log(1 - D(x))]$.
The generator wants to minimize the same quantity, trying to push $D(G(z))$ towards 1, i.e., fool the discriminator.
The combined objective is the minimax game $\min_G \max_D V(D, G) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]$.
This is not ordinary optimisation; it is a zero-sum game where two players are competing.
In principle, finding an equilibrium in a zero-sum game is much harder than a simple minimisation.
However, the structure of the GAN problem makes finding an equilibrium feasible.
For a fixed generator, the optimal discriminator is given by $D^*_G(x) = \frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_{\text{data}}(x) + p_g(x)}$.
Plugging the optimal discriminator into the value function yields the Jensen–Shannon divergence between $p_{\text{data}}$ and $p_g$.

The Jensen–Shannon divergence is defined as $\mathrm{JSD}(p_{\text{data}} \| p_g) = \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\text{data}} \;\middle\|\; \frac{p_{\text{data}}+p_g}{2}\right) + \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_g \;\middle\|\; \frac{p_{\text{data}}+p_g}{2}\right)$.
At the global minimum of the GAN game, the generator's distribution equals the data distribution: $p_g = p_{\text{data}}$.
The theoretical generator loss $\mathbb{E}_z[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]$ is very poor for training the generator in practice.
The problem is sigmoid-saturated cross-entropy.
When the discriminator becomes good at separating real from fake, it gives confident predictions with $D(G(z)) \approx 0$.
In that case, the gradient of $\log(1-D)$ saturates and nearly vanishes.
Then backpropagation through $D$ provides almost no signal to $G$, exactly when the generator needs to improve the most.
The practical fix is to use a non-saturating loss for the generator: minimize $-\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log D(G(z))]$.
This means maximizing the probability that the discriminator makes a mistake, rather than minimizing the probability of its correct answer.
This non-saturating loss keeps the gradient alive when the discriminator is strong.
Training of GANs proceeds in alternation, much like an EM algorithm.
Step 1: Fix $G$ and update $D$ by improving the binary cross-entropy on mini-batches of real data and generated data.
Step 2: Fix $D$ and update $G$ using the non-saturating loss.
In practice, the discriminator is often updated more frequently, or the updates are carefully balanced to avoid one network overpowering the other too quickly.
The original GAN (2014) produced reasonable digits on MNIST but struggled with diverse, natural images.
A major advance was Deep Convolutional GANs (DCGANs).
DCGANs replaced fully-connected layers with convolutional/deconvolutional architectures.
DCGANs used strided convolutions instead of pooling.
DCGANs added batch normalization everywhere.
DCGANs were trained with the Adam optimizer.
After only a few epochs on a dataset such as LSUN bedrooms, DCGAN could produce recognizable images of size 64×64 or 128×128.
These DCGAN results were state-of-the-art a decade ago.
These results already hinted at the latent space structure.
To tell if a generator has learned a meaningful mapping and not just memorized training examples, a visual test is used.
The discriminator cannot answer whether the generator has learned a meaningful mapping.
The discriminator's inability to distinguish real from generated merely indicates it is not powerful enough or not well trained.
A widely used visual test is a linear walk in the latent space.
The generator can be thought of as a map from a simple latent distribution $Z$, such as a standard Gaussian, to a point $X$ on the complicated manifold of real images.
To generate new images, we need to be able to sample a random $z$ and land reliably on the real image manifold.
In a linear walk, two latent vectors $z_1$ and $z_2$ that both produce plausible images are interpolated linearly.
Every intermediate point of the linear interpolation should also produce a plausible image.
If the images blur or morph unrealistically during interpolation, the manifold is not well flattened.
Good DCGANs show smooth, realistic transitions during linear walks in latent space.
Smooth latent walks confirm that the latent space is well-behaved and that sampling from the prior yields reasonable outputs.
Early GANs, including DCGAN, exhibited characteristic failures stemming from the local receptive fields of convolution.
The generator builds an image part by part with limited global context.
One failure mode is counting problems, such as three-headed dogs or multiple eyes.
Counting problems occur because the model does not know how many of a repeated feature to produce, since it only sees a small neighborhood.
Another failure mode is perspective inconsistencies, where different halves of an object may be rendered from different viewpoints.
Perspective inconsistencies occur because the generator has no global 3D understanding.
These mistakes are easy for humans to spot.
These mistakes reflect the difficulty of enforcing global coherence with purely local operations.
A crucial idea for scaling up resolution in GANs is to not generate the whole image at once.
Progressive Growing GAN (ProGAN) trains a GAN in stages.
ProGAN starts from $4 \times 4$ pixels and progressively adds layers that quadruple the resolution up to $1024 \times 1024$.
At each stage, new convolutional layers are added smoothly to both the generator and the discriminator.
This approach allows the model to first learn large-scale structure and then refine it.
Training time is saved because the early stages see many more lower-resolution images.
After about two weeks of training on powerful hardware, ProGAN produced the first high-resolution, photo-realistic human faces.
These faces are known from the website "ThisPersonDoesNotExist".
At the time, ProGAN incorporated improved loss functions.
One improved loss function was the Least Squares GAN (LSGAN).
LSGAN replaces the sigmoid cross-entropy with a squared-deviation target.
The LSGAN discriminator loss is $\min_D \frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{p_{\text{data}}}[(D(x)-b)^2] + \frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{p_z}[(D(G(z))-a)^2]$.
The LSGAN generator loss is $\min_G \frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{p_z}[(D(G(z))-c)^2]$.
Typical choices for LSGAN are $a=0$, $b=c=1$.
Because the LSGAN loss penalizes overshooting, nothing explodes to infinity, and gradients remain useful.

The deeper reason why standard divergences cause trouble in generative modeling is that $p_{\text{data}}$ and $p_g$ are concentrated on low-dimensional manifolds inside the high-dimensional pixel space.
The support of a realistic cat photo set is a tiny, intricate surface in $\mathbb{R}^{3\mathrm{M}}$.
The generator maps a low-dimensional noise vector to an image, so its distribution $p_g$ also lies on some low-dimensional manifold.
In the beginning of training, these two manifolds almost surely do not intersect; their overlap has measure zero.

In the Kullback-Leibler divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}} \| p_g) = \int p_{\text{data}}(x) \log \frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_g(x)}\,dx$, where $p_{\text{data}}(x) > 0$, we typically have $p_g(x) = 0$.
Thus the logarithm becomes infinite, making the KL divergence undefined or infinite.
This yields no useful gradient to move $p_g$ towards $p_{\text{data}}$.
Classical machine learning avoids this problem by adding Gaussian noise to the model, smoothing its support everywhere.
But in implicit generative models, we cannot remove that noise during generation, because adding noise blurs the images and defeats the purpose.
The Earth Mover distance (Wasserstein-1) provides a solution to the manifold mismatch problem.
Intuitively, think of the two probability distributions as piles of earth of total volume 1.
The Wasserstein distance is the minimum amount of work needed to turn one pile into the other, where work is approximately mass times distance moved.

Formally, $W(p_{\text{data}}, p_g) = \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(p_{\text{data}}, p_g)} \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim \gamma}[\|x - y\|]$, where $\Pi(p_{\text{data}}, p_g)$ is the set of joint distributions whose marginals are $p_{\text{data}}$ and $p_g$.
Crucially, the Wasserstein distance remains continuous and provides meaningful gradients even when the supports of the distributions are disjoint.
Moving a distribution a little bit closer always reduces the Earth Mover distance, whereas the KL divergence would still be infinite.
Computing the infimum over joint distributions in the Wasserstein distance seems intractable.

The Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality transforms the Wasserstein distance into a supremum over 1-Lipschitz functions: $W(p_{\text{data}}, p_g) = \sup_{\|f\|_L \le 1} (\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g}[f(x)])$.
We can parametrize $f$ with a neural network $f_w$, called the critic, because it no longer does binary classification.
Originally, the Lipschitz constraint was enforced by weight clipping to a small range.
In WGAN training, for a fixed generator, the critic is trained to maximize the difference of expectations, approximating the Wasserstein distance.
For a fixed critic, the generator's gradient is computed as $-\mathbb{E}_{z}[\nabla_\theta f_w(G_\theta(z))]$, and the generator is updated.
The WGAN loss correlates much better with image quality than the standard GAN loss.
The WGAN critic can be trained to convergence, unlike the discriminator in a standard GAN.
Weight clipping can cause the critic to learn over-simplified functions and may lead to exploding or vanishing gradients.
Improved WGAN (WGAN-GP) replaces weight clipping with a soft gradient penalty.

The gradient penalty term is $\lambda \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x} \sim P_{\hat{x}}}[(\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1)^2]$, where $\hat{x}$ is sampled uniformly along straight lines between real and generated samples.
This gradient penalty encourages the critic's gradient norm to stay close to 1 everywhere.
This enforces the Lipschitz condition in a gentler way and yields more stable training.
Further improvements in GANs addressed the locality of convolutions and scaled up the models.
Self‑Attention GAN (SAGAN) adds a Transformer‑like self‑attention mechanism over image features.
This self‑attention mechanism lets the generator capture long‑range dependencies.
The attention maps of SAGAN show that the network looks far across the image when synthesising fine details.
BigGAN combined self‑attention with very large architectures and careful regularisation.
BigGAN improved the Inception score threefold.
BigGAN produced high‑fidelity interpolations, such as smoothly morphing a bird into a dog with plausible intermediate hybrids.
Evaluating image quality itself is non‑trivial.
The Inception score is a commonly used metric.
To compute the Inception score, one takes a generated image $x$ and runs a pre‑trained Inception classifier to get $p(y \mid x)$.
The Inception score is defined as $\mathrm{IS} = \exp\!\Bigl( \mathbb{E}_x \,\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p(y \mid x) \,\|\, p(y)\bigr) \Bigr)$.
In the Inception score formula, $p(y)$ is defined as $p(y) = \int p(y \mid G(z))\, dz$.

The Inception score rewards images that are confidently classified as a particular class (low entropy in $p(y \mid x)$) while the generated set as a whole is diverse across classes (high entropy in $p(y)$).
A natural way to obtain a loss function for generation is to train an autoencoder.
In an autoencoder, an encoder maps an image $x$ to a latent code $z$.
In an autoencoder, a decoder maps $z$ back to a reconstruction $\hat{x}$.
Training an autoencoder minimises $\|x - \hat{x}\|^2$.
After training an autoencoder, the decoder alone can function as a generator by feeding it a latent code $z$ to get an image.
The aggregated posterior distribution of latent codes produced by the autoencoder's encoder on real data is complicated and not easy to sample from.
Simply drawing $z$ from a standard Gaussian and feeding it to the autoencoder's decoder will almost certainly miss the correct manifold, producing garbage.
An Adversarial Autoencoder (AAE) solves the sampling problem by adding a discriminator in the latent space.
In an AAE, the discriminator learns to distinguish between latent codes from the encoder (from real data) and samples from a simple prior (e.g., a standard Gaussian).
In an AAE, the encoder is simultaneously trained to fool the discriminator, pushing its output distribution to match the prior.
Once an AAE is trained, sampling $z$ from the Gaussian and passing it through the decoder yields plausible images.
AAEs can be extended to conditional generation by providing a label to the encoder and decoder.
AAEs can be extended to semi‑supervised learning.
VAEs offer a cleaner probabilistic regularisation compared to AAEs.
AAEs are a direct, adversarial alternative to VAEs.
AAEs still see use.
In Conditional GANs, the generator receives both a noise vector and a conditioning input (e.g., a class label, a low‑resolution image, or an age descriptor).
Conditional GANs enable tasks such as face ageing and super‑resolution (e.g., ESRGAN).
Stacked GANs (SGAN) are a chain of GANs where later stages condition on the output of earlier ones, progressively refining the representation through a hierarchy.
GANs were the state‑of‑the‑art for unconditional image generation until around 2020.
GANs remain strong in specific niches, such as super‑resolution, style transfer, and any domain where an explicit density is not needed.
For text‑to‑image generation and large‑scale prompted image synthesis, diffusion models have taken over.
The principle of adversarial training is still embedded in many modern pipelines.
The next lecture will introduce diffusion models and show how they connect to the ideas discussed today.
